title: The Definite Article
subtitle: אל = ال — "the"
intro: Arabic has one word for "the": al-, written אל in Judeo-Arabic. It attaches to the front of the noun as a single unit. Once you can spot it, a huge share of every page resolves into "the X" — and you'll see why so many First-50 words begin with אל.

sections.heading: One prefix, always attached
sections.body: Unlike Hebrew ה־, the article is the two letters אל glued to the front of the noun. Saadia writes the noun and its article as one word.

examples.note: The ארץ׳ you already know — with the article.

sections.heading: Sun letters: written, not always said
sections.body: Before about half the letters — the "sun letters" (ת ث ד ذ ר ז ס ש צ ض ط ظ ל נ) — the ל of אל assimilates in speech to the following sound, even though it is still written. So אלשמס is spelled with a lamed but pronounced ash-shams, not al-shams.

examples.note: Sun letter ש: the ל is written but assimilates → ash-shams.

sections.heading: Moon letters: said as written
sections.body: Before the other letters — the "moon letters" (א ב ג ח ך ע ף ק etc.) — the ל is both written and pronounced. אלקמר is simply al-qamar.

examples.note: Moon letter ק → al-qamar (the word that names the whole class).

quiz.explanation: אל = al- = "the", written as one unit with the noun.
ש is a sun letter, so the ל assimilates: ash-shams (still written with lamed).

quiz.q: Which one has an assimilating (sun-letter) article?
quiz.explanation: ר is a sun letter → ar-rabb. The others (ק, ב, כ) are moon letters, pronounced al-.
ק is a moon letter, so the ל is pronounced: al-qamar, "the moon."

quiz.q: Strip the article: what is the bare noun in אלארץ׳?
